ddx.step1_summary:
- Chief complaint: Recurrent episodes of right-hand pins-and-needles and transient right arm weakness with associated transient leg weakness / abnormal gait over the last 1–2 months.
- Onset/duration/severity: Symptoms began ~1–2 months ago. Initially infrequent (monthly) and brief, now happening up to a few times per day. Each episode lasts a few days and then resolves completely. Recently noted worsening (difficulty holding a cup during episodes). Fatigue and intermittent nausea reported. No current symptoms at time of consultation.
- Aggravating/alleviating factors: Episodes appear to arise spontaneously; no clear triggers identified. Symptoms resolve between episodes.
- Past medical history: None reported. Patient reports prior screening (BP, cholesterol, diabetes) was normal.
- Medications/allergies: Self-started aspirin 75 mg once daily (not prescribed). Allergy: penicillin.
- Family/social history: Father had carotid surgery (carotid endarterectomy) for stroke risk. Patient is a 32-year-old male doctor, lives with wife, non-smoker, works in plastic surgery.
- Vital signs / exam findings: No objective exam recorded in transcript; patient was asymptomatic during consultation. No focal deficits documented on exam due to teleconsultation.
- Labs / imaging: No new labs or imaging done in this consultation. Past screening for diabetes, BP, cholesterol reportedly normal. No brain or vascular imaging yet.
- Other relevant points: Episodes include sensory (paresthesia), motor (weakness) and some brainstem-type symptoms (sensation of lump in throat, nausea, transient difficulty holding cup). Neurology referral (TIA clinic) was arranged urgently by GP to exclude transient ischemic attack/stroke.

V: Transient ischemic attack / minor stroke: Unilateral intermittent focal neurological deficits (right-sided sensory and motor symptoms, gait change) could represent brief cerebral ischemia; family history of carotid disease increases concern.
Carotid stenosis / embolic disease: Family history of carotid surgery and focal lateralized symptoms raise remote possibility of arterial stenosis/embolism causing recurrent TIAs.
I: Transverse myelitis/post-infectious myelitis: Can cause focal limb weakness and sensory changes that evolve over days and can be monophasic or recurring in some inflammatory conditions.
Lyme or other CNS infection: Rare but can cause focal neurological signs; less likely without systemic infectious features.
N: Brain or cervical spinal cord tumor (focal lesion): A space-occupying lesion can cause focal sensory and motor deficits and gait changes; typically progressive rather than relapsing-remitting but could present variably.
D: Multiple sclerosis (demyelinating disease): Classically presents in young adults with relapsing-remitting focal neurological deficits (sensory symptoms, limb weakness, gait disturbance, fatigue) lasting days to weeks — fits time course and patient age.
I2: Iatrogenic/antithrombotic complication (aspirin-related bleeding): Chronic aspirin could increase bleeding risk, but episodic, resolving focal deficits are less typical for an intracranial hemorrhage.
Medication-related side effect (e.g., toxins): Unlikely given medication list, but substance/toxin exposures were not described.
C: Arteriovenous malformation (AVM) or vascular malformation: Could produce transient focal deficits or bleeding episodes, though less likely to present with multiple short, resolving episodes without acute deterioration.
A: Autoimmune neuromuscular disorder (e.g., myasthenia gravis): Fluctuating weakness and difficulty holding a cup could suggest neuromuscular junction disorder, but presence of sensory paresthesia and unilateral focal signs argue against classic myasthenia.
Autoimmune demyelination (e.g., MS) listed here as well: immune-mediated demyelination fits relapsing sensory/motor findings.
T: Cervical spine injury/radiculopathy: Cervical radiculopathy can produce unilateral hand paresthesia and arm weakness; less likely to cause leg/gait involvement without cord compression.
E: Electrolyte disturbance / periodic paralysis (e.g., hypokalemic periodic paralysis): Can cause episodic weakness, but usually symmetric proximal weakness without sensory symptoms; less consistent with this presentation.
Thyrotoxic periodic paralysis or metabolic disturbance: unlikely given sensory symptoms and episodic focal lateralized deficits.

step3_ranked_ddx.explanation: Young adult with relapsing-remitting focal neurological deficits (unilateral hand paresthesia, transient arm weakness, intermittent leg/gait disturbance), fatigue, and episodes lasting days with full resolution — classic pattern for MS.
supporting_evidence: Relapsing–remitting course over 1–2 months with focal sensory and motor deficits separated in time.
Symptoms last days and fully resolve between episodes (common in demyelinating events).
Associated fatigue and transient nausea (nonspecific but common in MS).
opposing_evidence: No prior neurological episodes documented before this timeframe (MS can still present with first episodes).
No objective neurological exam findings recorded (patient was asymptomatic at consult).
No MRI or CSF data yet to confirm demyelination.

step3_ranked_ddx.diagnosis: Hemiplegic migraine (complex migraine with motor aura)
step3_ranked_ddx.explanation: Migrainous aura can cause unilateral sensory symptoms, motor weakness lasting hours to days and associated nausea; episodic, transient deficits and nausea fit, though visual symptoms or headache were not clearly reported.
supporting_evidence: Nausea reported during symptomatic periods (common with migraine).
Episodic transient focal neurological symptoms lasting hours to days.
Difficulty holding a cup (transient motor dysfunction) during episodes consistent with motor aura.
opposing_evidence: No history of headache/headache not reported in transcript — hemiplegic migraine usually accompanies or is associated with headache.
Family history not suggestive of hemiplegic migraine; motor aura is less common than sensory/visual aura.
Frequency increasing to multiple times per day is atypical for classic hemiplegic migraine.

step3_ranked_ddx.diagnosis: Transient ischemic attack (TIA) / recurrent TIAs from vascular cause
step3_ranked_ddx.explanation: Unilateral focal neurological deficits raise concern for transient cerebral ischemia; family history of carotid disease prompted GP to refer urgently to TIA clinic. However patient age and duration of episodes (days) make classical TIA less typical.
supporting_evidence: Lateralized sensory and motor deficits (right-sided) that are transient.
Family history of carotid artery disease/stroke.
GP appropriately concerned and referred urgently to TIA clinic.
opposing_evidence: TIAs typically last minutes to hours and resolve within 24 hours; episodes here last several days, which is atypical.
Young patient without known vascular risk factors (prior screening normal for BP, cholesterol, diabetes).
No focal neurological deficits were present at time of assessment and no imaging/lab evidence yet.

step3_ranked_ddx.diagnosis: Cervical spinal cord pathology (e.g., compressive myelopathy, transverse myelitis)
step3_ranked_ddx.explanation: Unilateral hand paresthesia with concurrent leg weakness/gait change could reflect a cervical cord or high cervical radicular process; inflammatory transverse myelitis can be subacute and produce sensory and motor deficits lasting days–weeks.
supporting_evidence: Combination of upper-limb sensory/motor symptoms with leg/gait involvement suggests pathology at/above cervical cord level.
Subacute time course (days) could fit inflammatory myelopathy.
opposing_evidence: Symptoms are relapsing-remitting with full recovery between episodes — transverse myelitis usually causes more sustained deficits rather than frequent, fully resolving episodes.
No neck pain, recent infection or systemic features reported.
No imaging or neurological exam documented to support cord compression or myelitis.

step3_ranked_ddx.explanation: Focal seizures can produce paresthesia and transient weakness (postictal Todd's paralysis), but recurrent events lasting days and accompanied by sensory-only and motor-only episodes without witnessed seizure activity make this less likely.
supporting_evidence: Episodic focal neurological deficits could reflect transient postictal states.
Transient focal motor dysfunction (difficulty holding cup) compatible with focal motor seizures or postictal paresis.
opposing_evidence: No reports of witnessed jerking, altered awareness, tongue biting, incontinence or abrupt stereotyped events typical of seizures.
Episodes last days and frequency increased to multiple times per day — not typical for postictal paralysis which resolves over hours to days but usually follows an identifiable seizure.
